title: MongoDB Transactions: ACID Across Documents
summary: A dense field guide to MongoDB multi-document transactions — sessions, snapshot isolation, read and write concern, causal consistency, retries, and the performance limits that decide when to use them.

chapters.title: Why Transactions Exist in MongoDB
points: Single-document writes are always atomic in MongoDB — no transaction needed for one document, however deeply nested
Embedding is the first-choice 'transaction': model related data in one document and atomicity is free
Multi-document transactions added in 4.0 (replica sets), extended to sharded clusters in 4.2
ACID definition applied to MongoDB: Atomicity (all writes commit or none), Consistency (schema/index constraints hold), Isolation (snapshot reads), Durability (write concern majority + journal)
Motivating example: transfer $100 between two accounts stored as separate documents — debit and credit must both land
Before 4.0 the workaround was the two-phase commit pattern implemented manually in application code with a pending state field
Transactions require a replica set or sharded cluster — standalone mongod cannot run them because there is no oplog-based replication protocol
Storage engine requirement: WiredTiger, which supplies MVCC and document-level concurrency
Rule of thumb: if you need transactions for most operations, the schema is probably relational-shaped and needs remodelling
Transactions are an escape hatch, not the default access pattern — MongoDB's design goal is to make them rarely necessary
Cost preview: a transaction holds a snapshot open, pins storage-engine resources, and adds a commit round-trip
Comparison: SQL databases assume transactions everywhere; MongoDB assumes document-level atomicity covers ~90% of cases

chapters.title: Sessions: The Container for Everything
points: A session (ServerSession) is a logical context on the server identified by a UUID (lsid) sent with every command
Transactions cannot exist without a session — session is the unit that carries transaction number and state
startSession() on the client returns a ClientSession; it is lazily bound to a server session from a pool
Every operation inside a transaction must explicitly pass the session object — forgetting it silently runs the op outside the transaction
Node example: const session = client.startSession(); then coll.insertOne(doc, { session })
Sessions must be ended: session.endSession() in finally, or use withSession/withTransaction which handle it
Server reaps idle sessions after localLogicalSessionTimeoutMinutes (default 30); an abandoned in-progress transaction is aborted on reap
transactionNumber (txnNumber) increments per transaction within a session and makes commands idempotent for retries
Sessions also power retryable writes and causal consistency, independent of transactions
One session runs at most one transaction at a time — no nesting, no parallel operations on the same session
Driver session pooling reuses server sessions, so startSession is cheap; do not cache one session across concurrent requests
Gotcha: a session created from one MongoClient cannot be used with a different client — driver throws
db.serverStatus().transactions and $listLocalSessions expose live session and transaction counts

chapters.title: Writing a Transaction: The Core API
points: Three primitives: session.startTransaction(), session.commitTransaction(), session.abortTransaction()
Preferred API is the callback form withTransaction(), which retries both TransientTransactionError and UnknownTransactionCommitResult automatically
Manual pattern: try { startTransaction(); ...ops with session...; await commitTransaction() } catch { await abortTransaction() } finally { endSession() }
withTransaction callback may run more than once — it must be idempotent and must not have side effects outside the database
Do not swallow errors inside the withTransaction callback; the driver needs the error to decide whether to retry
Transaction options set at start: readConcern, writeConcern, readPreference, maxCommitTimeMS
readPreference inside a transaction must be primary — secondary reads in transactions are not supported
Aborting rolls back all writes; committing applies them atomically as a single oplog entry (or applyOps chain)
Nothing written in a transaction is visible to other sessions until commit — readers see the pre-transaction state
Reads inside the transaction do see the transaction's own uncommitted writes (read-your-own-writes within the txn)
Allowed operations: insert, update, delete, findAndModify, and most aggregation stages
Disallowed inside transactions: creating/dropping collections implicitly (pre-4.4), index builds, $out, $merge, listCollections-style metadata commands, count
Use countDocuments() instead of count() inside a transaction
Retry loop must be bounded — withTransaction stops retrying after 120 seconds of wall-clock time

chapters.title: Write Concern: Durability You Choose
points: Write concern answers 'how many nodes acknowledged before the driver returns'
Syntax: { w, j, wtimeout } — w = node count or tag, j = journal flush, wtimeout = milliseconds before error
w: 1 — primary only; fast, but a failover can roll the write back
w: 'majority' — durable across an election; default since MongoDB 5.0
w: 0 — fire and forget, no acknowledgement, no error reporting; only for throwaway telemetry
j: true forces an fsync of the journal on each acknowledging node before responding
wtimeout does NOT abort the write — it only stops waiting; the write may still replicate afterward
A transaction's write concern applies to the commit, not to each individual operation inside it
Setting write concern on an operation inside a transaction is an error — set it on the transaction or the commit
Custom write concerns via replica set tag sets, e.g. w: 'multiDC' requiring acknowledgement in two data centres
Tuning trade-off: w: 'majority' + j: true is the safest and the slowest; latency tracks the slowest majority-forming node
writeConcernMajorityJournalDefault controls whether majority implies journalling
Failure mode: w greater than the number of data-bearing voting members blocks until wtimeout, then errors
Interaction: readConcern 'majority' is only meaningful if writes actually reach a majority

chapters.title: Read Concern: Which Version You See
points: Read concern answers 'how fresh and how durable must the data I read be'
'local' — latest data on the queried node; may be rolled back; default outside transactions
'available' — like local but skips shard orphan filtering; lowest latency, can return orphaned documents
'majority' — only data acknowledged by a majority; never rolled back; default read concern inside transactions
'linearizable' — reflects all writes majority-acknowledged before the read started; primary only, single-document queries, must be combined with maxTimeMS
'snapshot' — a consistent point-in-time view across all documents and shards; available inside transactions and for causally consistent sessions
majority vs linearizable: majority can return stale data from a lagging node; linearizable pays a no-op write round-trip to prove primacy
snapshot read concern is what gives a transaction its repeatable reads — the same query returns the same result twice inside the transaction
Snapshot age is bounded by transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds (default 60) and the WiredTiger history store
Read concern set at transaction start applies to every read in the transaction; it cannot be changed per-operation
Comparison table row — local: fast/rollbackable, majority: durable/slightly stale, snapshot: consistent across docs, linearizable: freshest/slowest
Reading with 'majority' does not guarantee reading your own write unless the session is causally consistent
Aggregation and change streams honour read concern too

chapters.title: Snapshot Isolation and the Write Conflict
points: WiredTiger uses MVCC: each transaction reads from a snapshot taken at its start timestamp
Isolation level is snapshot isolation, not full serializability — write skew anomalies are possible
Write conflict: if another committed write touched a document after your snapshot began, your write fails with WriteConflict (code 112)
Outside a transaction, WiredTiger retries write conflicts internally and invisibly; inside a transaction the whole transaction aborts
WriteConflict surfaces to the driver as a TransientTransactionError, so withTransaction retries the whole callback
Design consequence: transactions on hot documents (a counter, a shared inventory row) degrade badly under contention
Anti-pattern example: every order transaction updating one global 'stats' document — serialized bottleneck
No read locks: readers never block writers and writers never block readers, unlike lock-based SQL engines
Contrast with PostgreSQL: default READ COMMITTED there, snapshot per statement; MongoDB transactions are snapshot per transaction
Write skew example: two transactions each check 'at least one doctor on call' and each removes a different doctor — both commit, invariant broken
Fix for write skew: force a shared write target so the conflict is detected, or use a unique index as a constraint
Transactions do take intent locks on collections and databases; a DDL operation can block or be blocked
maxTransactionLockRequestTimeoutMillis (default 5ms) controls how long a transaction waits for a lock before aborting

chapters.title: Causal Consistency: Read Your Own Writes
points: Causal consistency guarantees operations are observed in an order respecting cause and effect
Concrete need: write to primary, then read from a secondary — without it the read may not see the write
Enabled per session: startSession({ causalConsistency: true }) — on by default in most drivers when a session is used
Mechanism: every response carries an operationTime and a cluster time; the driver stores them and sends them back with afterClusterTime on the next read
Server holds the read until its oplog has applied up to that afterClusterTime, then serves it
Requires readConcern 'majority' for the full guarantee; with 'local' the causally-read data can still be rolled back
Four guarantees delivered: read your own writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, writes follow reads
Only holds within one session — two different sessions are not causally related unless you propagate cluster time manually
Propagating across services: pass session.getClusterTime() / operationTime through your API and call advanceClusterTime / advanceOperationTime on the receiving session
Gossiping cluster time is how nodes converge; $clusterTime is signed to prevent a client forging a future time
Cost: a causally consistent secondary read may block waiting for replication, trading latency for correctness
Does not apply to w: 0 writes — there is no operationTime to wait for
Transactions are causally consistent by construction; causal consistency is the cheaper option when you only need ordering, not atomicity

chapters.title: Sharded Cluster Transactions
points: Since 4.2 a transaction can span multiple shards; mongos coordinates it
Two-phase commit: one participating shard is elected transaction coordinator, sends prepare, collects votes, then commits or aborts
Prepared transactions write a prepare oplog entry; the coordinator's decision is durable in config.transaction_coordinators
A single-shard transaction skips two-phase commit entirely and costs about the same as a replica set transaction
Cost model: latency roughly grows with the number of participating shards; keep transactions single-shard where possible
Shard key design is the lever — co-locate documents that must change together so the transaction touches one shard
Distributed transactions require readConcern snapshot or majority/local; snapshot uses a global cluster-wide timestamp
A shard cannot be added to a transaction after the commit begins
Chunk migrations conflicting with an in-flight transaction cause the transaction to abort
In-progress prepared transactions block chunk migration and some DDL until they resolve
Sharded transactions cannot use readPreference secondary
Failure mode: a killed mongos leaves the coordinator to finish; the client gets UnknownTransactionCommitResult and must retry the commit
Monitor with db.serverStatus().transactions.totalPrepared and twoPhaseCommitCoordinator metrics

chapters.title: Errors, Retries, and Limits
points: Two error labels drive retry logic: TransientTransactionError and UnknownTransactionCommitResult
TransientTransactionError — the whole transaction is safe to retry from the beginning (write conflict, primary stepdown, NoSuchTransaction)
UnknownTransactionCommitResult — the commit may or may not have applied; retry commitTransaction, not the whole transaction
Retrying commit is safe because txnNumber makes it idempotent
withTransaction implements both loops; hand-rolled retries usually get UnknownTransactionCommitResult wrong
transactionLifetimeLimitSeconds default 60 — a transaction older than this is aborted by a periodic cleanup thread
Exceeding the limit yields 'Transaction with { txnNumber } has been aborted' — the fix is smaller transactions, not a bigger limit
16 MB oplog entry limit applied to the transaction's total writes (pre-4.2); 4.2+ splits into multiple oplog entries but the cap on individual documents still stands
maxTimeMS on operations and maxCommitTimeMS on the commit bound the wall-clock cost
Transactions abort automatically on primary stepdown, election, or session reap
Killing a long transaction: killSessions or killOp on the transaction's opid
Do not put network calls, user input, or long computation between startTransaction and commit — the snapshot ages the whole time
Idempotency requirement: because callbacks re-run, generate ObjectIds outside the callback if you need stable ids

chapters.title: Performance, Patterns, and Pitfalls
points: Rule 1: model to avoid transactions — embed, or accept eventual consistency, before reaching for a transaction
Rule 2: keep transactions short — under 1000 documents and well under 60 seconds is the practical guidance
Rule 3: keep transactions narrow — fewer collections and fewer shards means fewer conflicts and less coordination
Index the fields your transaction filters on; a collection scan inside a transaction holds the snapshot open far longer
Alternatives worth choosing instead: single-document atomic operators ($inc, $push, $set), findAndModify, the outbox pattern, or an idempotent job queue
Optimistic concurrency without transactions: a version field plus an update filtered on that version, retried on zero modified count
Common mistake: forgetting to pass the session to one operation — that write commits immediately and is not rolled back on abort
Common mistake: doing the retry loop by hand and retrying the whole transaction on a commit-unknown error, double-applying writes
Common mistake: creating a collection implicitly inside a transaction on older servers — pre-4.4 this is an error
Common mistake: leaking sessions by skipping endSession, exhausting the server session pool
Common mistake: assuming a transaction gives serializability — it gives snapshot isolation, so write skew still bites
Monitoring: watch transactions.currentActive, currentInactive, totalAborted, and WiredTiger cache pressure from long-lived snapshots
Benchmark reality: single-shard transactions cost roughly a normal write plus one commit round-trip; multi-shard commits multiply that
Closing checklist: session passed everywhere, withTransaction used, readConcern and writeConcern set deliberately, transaction short, hot documents avoided
